analysis.one_liner: Adds a 10% tax on income above $2 million a year ($1 million for single filers).
analysis.headline: A bill to add a 10% tax on income above $2 million ($1 million for singles) was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never advanced; no vote was taken.
analysis.plain_summary: The Millionaires Surtax Act would add a new 10% federal tax on a household's adjusted gross income above $2 million ($1 million for single filers), on top of existing income taxes. It applies to all income, including investment income, and would take effect for tax years after 2026. The money would go to the Treasury like other tax revenue. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has sat with no hearing, no vote, and no movement.
analysis.who_benefits: The direct beneficiaries would be everyone who does not pay it: the surtax targets only households with adjusted gross income above $2 million ($1 million for singles), a small share of taxpayers. Any revenue raised would flow to the Treasury for general federal spending, which ordinary taxpayers share in; whether it funds popular programs or deficit reduction would depend on later legislation.

how_it_helps.text: The bill imposes a 10% surtax on modified adjusted gross income above $2 million for joint filers and $1 million for everyone else, so only households with seven-figure incomes would pay anything.
The surtax applies to investment income as well as wages, hitting the main income source of the very wealthy, and applies to estates and trusts above the threshold.
The revenue would be available for any federal purpose, so it could fund services or deficit reduction that benefit ordinary taxpayers.

analysis.who_pays: Households with modified adjusted gross income above $2 million ($1 million for singles), including income from investments, businesses, and trusts; their tax bills would rise by up to 10% of income above the threshold.

drawbacks.text: The surtax applies to all income above the threshold, including business and investment income of people who might respond by shifting earnings, moving income abroad, or restructuring their affairs, which could erode the revenue it raises.
A surtax on high earners may be partly passed through to the economy in other forms, and its revenue benefit depends on IRS enforcement against well-advised taxpayers.
As introduced with only three co-sponsors and no Senate or House vote, the bill offered its supporters no realistic path to becoming law in this Congress.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The surtax is broad (all income above the threshold, not just wages) and straightforward to administer, and its cost falls entirely on households with seven-figure incomes, a small group with substantial ability to pay. Honest drawbacks: it may push some investment activity abroad, depends on an IRS that must police sophisticated avoidance, and its revenue could be spent rather than saved. It was never drafted with compromise, so the objections above never got answered.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it sat with no hearing, no vote, and no floor action for the rest of the session so far.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 15, 2026, and read twice on the Senate floor the same day.
It was then referred to the Senate Committee on Finance, where tax legislation must be approved before reaching the full Senate.
No further action has been taken: no committee vote, no floor vote, and no companion action has been recorded since introduction.
The bill attracted three Democratic co-sponsors and no Republican support.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Households earning over $2 million are better off, because the 10% surtax on their income above that level never advanced. Lawmakers who preferred not to take a position also avoided a recorded vote.

for.name: Sen. Chris Van Hollen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and secured three Democratic co-sponsors.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee (majority needed to act)
against.what_they_did: Took no action: no hearing, markup, or vote was scheduled on the bill after referral.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors and co-sponsors are Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the bill never reached a vote.

industries.note: These households would pay a new 10% surtax on all income above the threshold, including investment income. They are the bill's only direct payers.

industries.industry: Tax advisory and wealth management services
industries.note: A new surtax on high earners would generate demand for tax planning to minimize it, while raising the stakes of tax advice for wealthy clients.

analysis.trajectory: Bills referred to Senate Finance with no hearings and no Republican co-sponsors rarely advance, especially tax increases on high earners; the realistic outlook is that the bill dies in committee when the Congress ends, unless its sponsors attach it to broader tax legislation.
